title: In Defence of Boredom
sourceNote: Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading (dạng bài nghị luận); dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu tâm lý học đã công bố.

sections.text: Boredom has a poor reputation. It is associated with idleness, restlessness and, in children, with bad behaviour, and an entire industry of entertainment now exists to ensure that we never have to experience it. Smartphones in particular have made it possible to fill every spare moment, whether we are waiting for a bus, standing in a queue or sitting in a doctor's surgery. Yet a growing body of psychological research suggests that this constant escape may come at a price. Boredom, it seems, is not simply an unpleasant state to be eliminated but a signal that serves a purpose, and occasionally it may even be good for us.

Defining boredom is harder than it sounds. The psychologist John Eastwood, of York University in Toronto, has described it as the uncomfortable experience of wanting to engage in a satisfying activity but being unable to do so. This definition helps to distinguish boredom from mere relaxation: a person lying contentedly on a beach is not bored, whereas a person stuck in a meeting that seems pointless very often is. More recently, Erin Westgate has proposed that boredom arises from two separate problems, namely a lack of meaning in what we are doing and a mismatch between the demands of a task and the attention we are able to give it.

How strongly do people wish to avoid this feeling? A striking answer came from a series of studies led by Timothy Wilson at the University of Virginia and published in 2014. Participants were asked to sit alone in a plain room for between six and fifteen minutes with nothing to do except think. Most reported that they found the experience unpleasant. In one version, participants were given the option of pressing a button that delivered a mild electric shock, which they had earlier said they would pay money to avoid. Remarkably, around two-thirds of the men and a quarter of the women chose to shock themselves at least once rather than simply sit with their thoughts.

If boredom is so aversive, could it ever be useful? The British psychologist Sandi Mann believes it can. In one experiment, she asked one group of volunteers to spend fifteen minutes copying numbers out of a telephone directory, a task chosen precisely because it was so tedious. Afterwards, they and a control group were asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Those who had endured the boring task came up with more ideas, and more original ones. Mann's explanation is that a dull activity encourages the mind to wander, and that daydreaming allows the brain to make unexpected connections between ideas.

This interpretation fits with research on what neuroscientists call the default mode network, a set of brain regions that becomes more active when we are not focused on an external task. Activity in this network has been linked with imagination, planning for the future and reflecting on our own experiences. The important point is that these processes appear to need unstructured time in which to operate. If every gap in the day is immediately filled with messages, videos and news, the mind may rarely enter this reflective state, and some of the benefits of an idle moment may be lost without our noticing. Some researchers believe that this is one reason why good ideas so often seem to arrive in the shower or on a long walk, when attention is free to drift.

None of this means that boredom should be welcomed uncritically. Chronic boredom, as opposed to the passing kind, is associated with depression, overeating and risky behaviour, and nobody would recommend that a pupil in an uninspiring lesson simply learn to enjoy the experience. The more modest claim is that occasional boredom is a normal part of life and that our determination to avoid it at all costs may be counterproductive. Adults who rush to entertain children the moment they complain of having nothing to do may, with the best of intentions, be depriving them of an opportunity to develop their own resources.

The philosopher Bertrand Russell made a similar point almost a century ago, warning that a generation unable to endure boredom would achieve little of lasting value. Russell could not have imagined the devices that now compete for our attention, but his warning seems more relevant than ever. Learning to tolerate a few minutes of emptiness, without reaching for a screen, may be a small but worthwhile discipline. Boredom tells us that something in our situation needs to change; if we silence that message too quickly, we may never discover what we might have done instead.

items.q: The widespread use of smartphones may have disadvantages that people do not realise.
items.e: Đoạn A: việc liên tục thoát khỏi sự nhàm chán bằng điện thoại 'may come at a price'; đoạn E nói lợi ích có thể mất 'without our noticing' → tác giả đồng ý → YES.

items.q: Chronic boredom is as beneficial as the occasional kind.
items.e: Đoạn F: nhàm chán kinh niên gắn với trầm cảm, ăn quá nhiều, hành vi rủi ro; tác giả chỉ bênh vực sự nhàm chán 'thỉnh thoảng' → trái ý tác giả → NO.

items.q: Schools should make lessons deliberately boring to encourage creativity.
items.e: Đoạn F: 'nobody would recommend that a pupil in an uninspiring lesson simply learn to enjoy the experience' – tác giả không ủng hộ để học sinh chịu đựng giờ học nhàm chán → NO.

items.q: Children today are more easily bored than children were in the past.
items.e: Bài không so sánh mức độ dễ chán của trẻ em ngày nay với trẻ em ngày xưa. Đoạn F chỉ nói người lớn vội giải trí cho trẻ → NOT GIVEN.

items.q: found that a dull task was followed by more creative thinking
items.e: Đoạn D: Sandi Mann cho một nhóm chép số danh bạ 15 phút, sau đó họ nghĩ ra nhiều công dụng của cốc nhựa hơn và độc đáo hơn → Sandi Mann.

items.q: suggested that boredom has two distinct causes
items.e: Đoạn B: Erin Westgate cho rằng nhàm chán đến từ 'two separate problems' – thiếu ý nghĩa và lệch giữa yêu cầu công việc với mức chú ý → Erin Westgate.

items.q: showed that many people prefer physical discomfort to being alone with their thoughts
items.e: Đoạn C: trong nghiên cứu của Timothy Wilson, khoảng 2/3 nam và 1/4 nữ tự sốc điện thay vì ngồi một mình suy nghĩ → Timothy Wilson.

items.q: predicted that people who could not cope with boredom would accomplish little
items.e: Đoạn G: Bertrand Russell cảnh báo một thế hệ không chịu nổi sự nhàm chán 'would achieve little of lasting value' → Bertrand Russell.

items.q: Eastwood's definition separates boredom from ______, such as lying happily on a beach.
items.e: Đoạn B: định nghĩa này giúp 'distinguish boredom from mere relaxation' – người nằm thư giãn trên bãi biển không chán → relaxation.

items.q: Participants could choose to press a button that delivered a mild ______.
items.e: Đoạn C: nút bấm 'delivered a mild electric shock' → electric shock.

items.q: Mann's volunteers spent fifteen minutes copying numbers out of a ______.
items.e: Đoạn D: nhóm tình nguyện viên 'copying numbers out of a telephone directory' → telephone directory.

items.q: Mann believes that a dull activity allows the mind to ______, helping the brain link ideas.
items.e: Đoạn D: 'a dull activity encourages the mind to wander' – để tâm trí lang thang → wander.

items.q: The default mode network is connected with imagination, reflection and planning for the ______.
items.e: Đoạn E: hoạt động của mạng này gắn với 'imagination, planning for the future and reflecting on our own experiences' → future.
